personas.summary: Chemically this is one of the strongest chapters I have reviewed. I independently re-parsed every SMILES in the package with RDKit: all 20 structures parse, and the InChIKeys of adenosine, 2'-deoxyadenosine, thymidine, cytidine, uridine, dAMP, ATP, zidovudine, acyclovir and the five free bases match the authentic compounds; beta-D-ribofuranose and 2-deoxy-beta-D-ribofuranose carry the same C1'/C3'/C4' configurations as the corresponding nucleosides, so the beta-anomeric and D-sugar claims are correct throughout; the dinucleotide really is dA(3'->5')dT with a free 5'-OH on the adenine residue and a free 3'-OH on the thymine residue; the uridine 2',3'-cyclic phosphate is a genuine cis-fused five-membered cyclic diester that embeds in 3D; the cAMP distractor in the RNA-cleavage question is a real 3',5'-cyclic phosphate; and both hotspot answer keys point at the chemically correct atom [redacted]. Base tautomers are uniformly the lactam form, donor/acceptor assignments along both pairing edges are right, N9/N1 attachment is right, 3'-to-5' directionality is right, the 2'-alkoxide/in-line/2',3'-cyclic-phosphate mechanism is right, and attack is correctly placed at the alpha phosphorus with pyrophosphate hydrolysis correctly identified as the driving force rather than the substitution itself. The prose repeatedly builds mechanistic 'why' rather than asserting outcomes, and the wrong-answer explanations are among the best in the corpus. My verdict is NOT-GO as it stands, for one narrow reason and a set of fixable gaps: the two strand-directionality questions name DNA residues as ribonucleosides ('the adenosine residue', 'the cytidine residue') inside the keyed-correct option, directly contradicting the rule the chapter itself teaches in its very first practice check, and one of their distractors places a 2'-oxygen on a DNA residue that cannot have one. Beyond that, the chapter never shows a base pair with its hydrogen bonds anywhere, never shows an arrow-pushing step for either of its two flagship mechanisms (all four video briefs are deferred with empty URLs), and the one figure in the advanced section compiles to an empty image. Fix the naming, and this is a go with those visual gaps scheduled.

location.anchor_text: The adenosine residue's 3'-oxygen is esterified to the linking phosphate

findings.observation: Both strand-directionality questions describe DNA residues using ribonucleoside names. In ch28-strand-directionality the strand is DNA, and both the keyed-correct option and a distractor misname the DNA residue with a ribonucleoside term ('adenosine' rather than '2'-deoxyadenosine'), and the distractor additionally describes a 2'-oxygen a DNA residue cannot have. In ch28-strand-directionality-v2 the same ribonucleoside-naming error recurs in the keyed-correct option. The correct compounds are 2'-deoxyadenosine and 2'-deoxycytidine. This contradicts the chapter's own teaching: the practice check on nugget-nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy states explicitly that a cytidine residue 'could not appear in DNA, because the sugar is D-ribose and still carries a 2'-hydroxyl', and the parallel practice check on nugget-phosphodiester-backbone gets the same molecule right by writing 'the 2'-deoxyadenosine residue'.
findings.learner_impact: A student who answers correctly is shown a confirmation that names a compound the chapter has just told them cannot exist in DNA, so the single most important structural distinction in the chapter (ribose vs 2'-deoxyribose, concept 1) is undermined by the assessment that follows it. A student who has internalised the rule will read the keyed answer as wrong and lose confidence in the bank; a student who has not will learn the wrong name from an autograded item.
findings.evidence: ch28-strand-directionality options a and c ('The adenosine residue's 3'-oxygen...', 'The adenosine residue's 2'-oxygen...'); ch28-strand-directionality-v2 option a ('Only the cytidine residue, because it sits at the right-hand end...'); versus nugget-nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy practice_check answer ('It could not appear in DNA, because the sugar is D-ribose and still carries a 2'-hydroxyl') and nugget-phosphodiester-backbone practice_check answer ('the 3'-hydroxyl of the 2'-deoxyadenosine residue').
findings.recommended_outcome: Every residue of a DNA strand must be named as the 2'-deoxy compound wherever the chapter names it, including inside option text and feedback, and the 2'-oxygen distractor needs to be either re-anchored on an RNA strand or replaced with a distractor that is possible for DNA, so that the assessment stops contradicting the chapter's own ribose/deoxyribose rule.

findings.observation: The chapter's headline skill is deriving A-T and G-C from the donor/acceptor pattern rather than memorising them, and the prose walks each edge position by position. But no representation anywhere in the chapter shows two bases facing each other with the hydrogen bonds drawn. The section's assets are the four isolated bases (mol-adenine, mol-thymine, mol-guanine, mol-cytosine), each rendered on its own; the only asset that could have shown a pair, video-base-pairing, has production_status 'deferred' and compiles into the reader as a video block with url '' and is_hidden true. The same is true of the mismatch cases (A opposite C, G opposite T) that the prose asks students to work through themselves.
findings.learner_impact: Reading 'the adenine NH2 reaches the thymine C4 oxygen while the thymine N3-H reaches adenine N1' and then being handed two separate molecules leaves the student to do the mental rotation and juxtaposition unaided. This is precisely the step where students substitute memorisation for derivation, which is the misconception the section is written to prevent, and the two rejected pairs (donor-against-donor, acceptor-against-acceptor) are almost impossible to see without a facing-pair depiction.
findings.evidence: nugget-base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding asset_ids = [mol-adenine, mol-thymine, mol-guanine, mol-cytosine]; video-base-pairing production_status 'deferred'; compiled reader section nugget-base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding contains one text block, four molecule blocks, one hidden video block and one link block, and no paired representation.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs a representation in which two bases sit in their pairing orientation with each hydrogen bond, donor and acceptor identified, including at least one of the rejected combinations - available to a student who never plays a video, since the video is deferred indefinitely.

findings.observation: Neither of the chapter's two mechanisms is drawn anywhere. For RNA cleavage the assets are uridine, uridine 2',3'-cyclic phosphate and the dinucleotide - start and end states with nothing between them - and the objective on that concept literally reads 'Draw the mechanism by which base cleaves an RNA backbone through the 2'-alkoxide and a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate intermediate', while the prose says 'it is worth drawing for yourself rather than reading'. For chain extension the assets are ATP, dAMP and the dinucleotide. Both video briefs that would have carried the arrows (video-rna-cleavage, video-chain-extension) are production_status 'deferred' and compile to hidden blocks with empty URLs. No curved-arrow, mechanism-path or reaction-coordinate asset exists in the package.
findings.learner_impact: In-line attack at phosphorus with a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement and inversion, and the geometric point that a nucleophile two atoms away is held in position by the furanose ring, are spatial claims that prose alone cannot carry. Students who cannot construct the arrows will fall back on memorising 'RNA has a 2'-OH so it is unstable' - exactly the non-mechanistic account the concept's trouble_spots warn against.
findings.evidence: nugget-rna-versus-dna-hydrolytic-stability learning_objectives[0]; expanded text 'it is worth drawing for yourself rather than reading'; video-rna-cleavage and video-chain-extension both production_status 'deferred'; assets[] contains no curved_arrow or mechanism asset type for this chapter.
findings.recommended_outcome: Both substitutions at phosphorus need a step-resolved arrow-pushing representation - nucleophile, in-line trajectory, leaving group, and for RNA the five-membered cyclic intermediate - available in the reader without depending on the deferred videos.

findings.observation: The synthesis_roadmap asset roadmap-phosphoramidite-cycle compiles into the reader as an image block whose url is the empty string. The section it serves - Sanger sequencing plus the four-step phosphoramidite cycle, the chapter's only multi-step synthetic sequence - therefore renders with a broken/empty figure followed by two molecule figures (dideoxyadenosine and dAMP) that illustrate the sequencing half but not the cycle at all. The roadmap's spec, notes and long_description are all well authored; only the rendered artefact is missing. (This is a recurring compile behaviour: carbonyl-alpha-substitution, alkynes-organic-synthesis, carboxylic-acids-and-nitriles and alkanes-and-stereochemistry show the same empty-image pattern.)
findings.learner_impact: The four operations of the cycle and their obligatory order - detritylate, couple, cap, oxidise - are the assessable content of this section (ch28-phosphoramidite-step-order asks exactly for that order), and students meet them only as running prose. Anyone scanning for a diagram sees an empty frame and concludes the figure failed to load.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/biomolecules-nucleic-acids.json, section nugget-reading-and-writing-dna, block blk-07do3m2b: {"url": "", "alt_text": "A four-step linear roadmap for adding one residue by phosphoramidite synthesis...", "caption": "One turn of the phosphoramidite synthesis cycle"}.
findings.recommended_outcome: The four-step cycle needs a figure that actually renders in the reader, or the roadmap must be replaced by a representation the compiler can emit; an empty image frame is worse for the student than no figure at all.

location.anchor_text: Working from the structures rather than from memory, which statement gives the reason it fails?

findings.observation: Several questions instruct the student to reason from structures but show none. ch28-mismatch-failure-mode says 'Working from the structures rather than from memory' and offers four text-only options. ch28-pairing-donors-acceptors says 'Select every statement below that reads that pattern correctly off the structures' and shows no structures. ch28-purine-pyrimidine-sort-v2 says 'Drawn in its predominant tautomer, each nucleic acid base either does or does not carry an exocyclic amino group' but presents five bare base names. ch28-chain-terminator-design asks the student to choose a C3' modification with no structure of thymidine present. The accessibility_bundle for each of these correctly records 'No structures are shown' / 'Text-only question', confirming the omission is real rather than a rendering issue.
findings.learner_impact: These items silently convert a structure-reading task into a recall task. A student who has learned the derivation is given no structure to derive from, and one who has memorised the pairs answers correctly without ever reading an edge - so the question no longer discriminates on the skill the chapter is trying to build.
findings.evidence: ch28-mismatch-failure-mode and ch28-pairing-donors-acceptors student_config.options contain no structure_smiles; ch28-purine-pyrimidine-sort student_config.items are name-only; contrast with ch28-base-pair-comparison and ch28-nucleoside-vs-nucleotide, which do carry structure_smiles on every option.
findings.recommended_outcome: Any question whose prompt tells the student to work from the structures must put those structures in front of them, so the assessed behaviour matches the instruction given.

location.anchor_text: Assign the beta configuration at the anomeric carbon and explain what beta means in terms of the face the base occupies relative to C5'.

findings.observation: The second learning objective of the N-glycosidic-bond concept - assign the beta configuration and say what beta means relative to C5' - is taught carefully in prose ('Because C1' is a stereocentre, this is a genuine stereochemical statement and not a naming convention: the alpha and beta nucleosides are diastereomers') but is assessed by none of the six questions on that concept (attachment site x2, depurination x2, acid/base stability x2), and no asset shows the alpha anomer for contrast. Every nucleoside figure in the package is beta, so the student never sees the thing beta is being distinguished from.
findings.learner_impact: Students can pass every item on this concept while carrying the misconception the concept's own trouble_spots list first: 'treating the anomeric configuration as a free choice rather than a fixed structural fact'. Without a contrast case and without an item that requires the assignment, 'beta' remains a word attached to every drawing rather than a stereochemical claim.
findings.evidence: concepts[].slug 'n-glycosidic-bond' learning_objectives[1]; question_sets with concept_slug 'n-glycosidic-bond' = ch28-glycosidic-attachment-site(+v2), ch28-depurination-short(+v2), ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability(+v2), none of which mentions alpha or beta; assets mol-adenosine, mol-2-deoxyadenosine, mol-thymidine, mol-cytidine are all beta.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs both a way to see the alpha and beta anomers side by side and at least one item that requires the student to assign or select the natural configuration, so the stated objective is actually exercised.

location.anchor_text: so a course short on time can teach the chapter's structural and mechanistic core without it and lose nothing that later material depends on

findings.observation: The teacher_optional metadata is internally inconsistent. nucleoside-analogue-drugs is marked teacher_optional with why_optional stating that dropping it loses 'nothing that later material depends on'. But reading-and-writing-dna lists nucleoside-analogue-drugs in its prerequisites, and its prose depends on it explicitly: 'add a small proportion of dideoxynucleoside triphosphates - the 2',3'-dideoxy analogues from the previous section'. An instructor who uses the removable-concept machinery to drop concept 9 while keeping concept 10 gets a section whose declared prerequisite is absent and whose text refers back to material the student never saw.
findings.learner_impact: Instructors trust why_optional when trimming a course. Acting on this one produces a Sanger-sequencing section that assumes a chain terminator the class has not met, and the sequencing rank_order question (ch28-phosphoramidite-step-order-v2) then asks about dideoxynucleoside triphosphates cold.
findings.evidence: concepts[8] nucleoside-analogue-drugs why_optional; concepts[9] reading-and-writing-dna prerequisites = ['chain-extension-at-phosphorus', 'nucleoside-analogue-drugs']; nugget-reading-and-writing-dna expanded text 'the 2',3'-dideoxy analogues from the previous section'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The optionality claim and the prerequisite graph must agree - either the two optional concepts need to be declared as a single removable unit, or the why_optional wording must stop promising that nothing downstream depends on concept 9.

location.anchor_text: The two sugar-phosphate strands of a duplex run at a fixed separation

findings.observation: Two concepts assume material they do not declare as prerequisites. base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding lists only purine-and-pyrimidine-bases, yet its central geometric argument is built on the sugar-phosphate backbone running at a fixed separation - that is phosphodiester-backbone material. chain-extension-at-phosphorus lists only phosphodiester-backbone, yet its expanded text repeatedly leans on the previous section: 'This is the same substitution-at-phosphorus chemistry as the RNA cleavage in the previous section, run constructively rather than destructively.' The linear reading order happens to satisfy both, so nothing breaks in the reader, but the declared graph is what drives concept maps, prerequisite checks and any non-linear assembly of these nuggets.
findings.learner_impact: Any surface that reorders or subsets concepts using prerequisites - concept maps, deck assembly, adaptive review - can present the base-pairing geometry argument before the backbone exists, or the chain-extension analogy before the reader has met substitution at phosphorus.
findings.evidence: concepts[4] base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding prerequisites = ['purine-and-pyrimidine-bases']; concepts[7] chain-extension-at-phosphorus prerequisites = ['phosphodiester-backbone']; nugget-base-pairing expanded 'The two sugar-phosphate strands of a duplex run at a fixed separation'; nugget-chain-extension expanded 'the same substitution-at-phosphorus chemistry as the RNA cleavage in the previous section'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The prerequisite lists need to name every concept the prose actually assumes, so the declared graph matches the argument the student is asked to follow.

location.anchor_text: of uracil uridine, and of thymine thymidine - purines take the ending -osine, pyrimidines take -idine. Prefix a nucleoside name with 2'-deoxy and you have named the DNA version

findings.observation: The naming rule as stated makes thymidine the ribonucleoside of thymine and 2'-deoxythymidine the DNA version. Everywhere else in the chapter - the mol-thymidine asset, the dinucleotide, zidovudine, and the matching question that keys 'Thymidine' to '2'-Deoxyribonucleoside of a pyrimidine' - the unprefixed name is used for the 2'-deoxy compound, which is the correct convention. The exception is stated exactly once, and only inside a wrong-answer explanation on ch28-sugar-and-base-identity-v2 ('By convention the unprefixed name thymidine already means the 2'-deoxy compound'), so a student sees it only if they get that item wrong.
findings.learner_impact: A student applying the reader's stated rule will conclude that thymidine carries a 2'-OH, then meet mol-thymidine (which does not) and a matching item that keys the opposite. Given that the ribose/deoxyribose distinction is the chapter's first concept and the axis on which several items turn, an unflagged nomenclature exception in the naming rule is a predictable source of wrong answers.
findings.evidence: nugget-nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy expanded text naming pattern; asset mol-thymidine SMILES Cc1cn([C@H]2C[C@H](O)[C@@H](CO)O2)c(=O)[nH]c1=O (2'-deoxy, InChIKey IQFYYKKMVGJFEH-XLPZGREQSA-N); ch28-sugar-and-base-identity answer_key l3->r1 ('2'-Deoxyribonucleoside of a pyrimidine'); the convention note appears only in ch28-sugar-and-base-identity-v2 feedback.
findings.recommended_outcome: The thymidine exception belongs in the reader prose where the naming rule is stated, not only in a wrong-answer explanation, so that the rule the student is given matches the names the rest of the chapter uses.

location.anchor_text: the OpenStax sections 28.1 to 28.8 map one to one onto the print McMurry sections

findings.observation: textbook_matching claims a one-to-one map onto McMurry/OpenStax chapter 28 and lists 'polymerase chain reaction' among its matching terms, and the compiled reader emits an mcmurry_link to https://openstax.org/books/organic-chemistry/pages/28-why-this-chapter. But no concept, nugget, asset or question in the package covers the polymerase chain reaction (OpenStax 28.8) or translation / protein biosynthesis (OpenStax 28.5). Chain extension does cover the chemistry common to replication and transcription, so 28.3 and 28.4 are served; PCR and translation are simply absent.
findings.learner_impact: An instructor assigning this chapter alongside McMurry or OpenStax chapter 28 will find two textbook sections with no ChemIllusion prose, figures or practice, after the package has told them the mapping is one to one. Students following the mcmurry_link land on a chapter containing PCR and will look for the corresponding ChemIllusion section.
findings.evidence: textbook_matching.terms includes 'polymerase chain reaction'; textbook_matching.overrides['openstax-organic-chemistry-current'].note 'the OpenStax sections 28.1 to 28.8 map one to one onto the print McMurry sections'; concepts[] contains no PCR or translation concept; grep of the package finds no occurrence of PCR, primer amplification or genetic code outside the Sanger-primer context.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the coverage gap needs closing for PCR (which is a direct application of the chain-extension chemistry already taught and would cost little) or the textbook-matching note must stop claiming a one-to-one mapping and say explicitly which textbook sections are out of scope.

location.anchor_text: Describe the B-form double helix: two antiparallel strands, a right-handed twist, bases stacked in the interior and the charged backbone outside.

findings.observation: Several stated objectives are taught but never assessed. The first objective of the double-helix concept - describe the B form, two antiparallel strands, right-handed, bases inside and backbone outside - is not touched by either question on that concept (ch28-duplex-stability-reasoning covers stacking, its v2 covers the grooves, and the two rank_order items cover melting). Antiparallelity, which the chapter argues is a structural necessity rather than a convention and which it links to leading/lagging strand synthesis, is assessed by no item in the bank. Similarly, the second objective of nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy ('State what the prime marks in a locant such as C3'') and the 'Draw the 3'-to-5' phosphodiester linkage' objective are assessed only by recognition items; the only structure_scaffold questions in the whole 46-item bank ask for thymine and uracil.
findings.learner_impact: An instructor using this bank as the chapter's assessment gets no evidence that students can describe the duplex, state why the strands must run antiparallel, or construct a phosphodiester linkage on paper - all of which the chapter's objectives promise. Recognition items on multi-part structural facts overstate mastery.
findings.evidence: concepts[5] dna-double-helix-and-base-stacking learning_objectives[0]; question_sets with that concept_slug = ch28-duplex-stability-reasoning(+v2), ch28-melting-temperature-rank(+v2); structure_scaffold questions in the bank = ch28-draw-thymine, ch28-draw-thymine-v2 only.
findings.recommended_outcome: The bank needs at least one item that requires the student to produce or assemble structure beyond a single base - a linkage, a nucleoside, or the antiparallel arrangement - so that the chapter's drawing and description objectives are actually evidenced.

location.anchor_text: Attacking it would cut the triphosphate between alpha and beta, delivering a phosphate group to the end of the growing chain

findings.observation: The wrong-answer explanation for selecting the beta phosphorus (atom_19) misstates the product. If the chain's 3'-oxygen attacks P-beta and expels the alpha-side bridging oxygen, the leaving group is the nucleoside 5'-monophosphate (correctly stated) but the group delivered to the chain end is a diphosphate carrying both the beta and the gamma phosphorus, not 'a phosphate group'. The corresponding explanation for gamma is correct as written ('transfers one phosphate: the chain end would be phosphorylated and the nucleoside diphosphate would drift away').
findings.learner_impact: Students working through the alpha/beta/gamma reasoning by bookkeeping - which the hints explicitly ask them to do ('Draw the product of attack at beta') - will find their own correct answer contradicted by the feedback, in the one place the chapter insists the atoms be tracked exactly.
findings.evidence: ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot feedback_bundle.wrong_answer_explanations, match region_ids contains atom_19.
findings.recommended_outcome: The beta-attack feedback needs its product bookkeeping corrected so it agrees with the arrow-pushing the hints ask the student to perform.

location.anchor_text: purine nucleosides undergo this hydrolysis far faster than pyrimidine nucleosides - by roughly two orders of magnitude under comparable conditions

findings.observation: The purine-over-pyrimidine rate ratio for N-glycosidic hydrolysis is given as 'roughly two orders of magnitude' in the nugget and repeated as 'by roughly two orders of magnitude' and 'by about a hundredfold' in the feedback of ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability-v2. The figure usually quoted for DNA is a factor of about 20 (depyrimidination proceeds at roughly 5 percent of the depurination rate), so the chapter overstates the ratio by about fivefold. The qualitative claim - purines are lost, pyrimidines largely stay - is correct and is what the questions actually turn on.
findings.learner_impact: Low: no item is keyed on the number. But the value is asserted three times with apparent precision, and a student who carries '100-fold' into a biochemistry course will be repeating a figure that does not match the standard one.
findings.evidence: nugget-n-glycosidic-bond expanded text; ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability-v2 generic_incorrect_explanation ('by roughly two orders of magnitude') and option-c explanation ('by about a hundredfold').
findings.recommended_outcome: Either soften the quantitative claim to the qualitative one the questions rely on, or bring the stated ratio into line with the value normally quoted for DNA.

location.anchor_text: exactly as a nucleophile approaches a carbon in an S_N2 reaction

findings.observation: The chapter uses two different renderings of the SN2 label. The expanded prose of nugget-rna-versus-dna-hydrolytic-stability writes 'S_N2' with a literal underscore, which is carried verbatim into the compiled reader markdown (two occurrences in frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/biomolecules-nucleic-acids.json) and will render either as raw 'S_N2' or with the underscore consumed as markdown emphasis. Elsewhere in the package - ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability option b and its feedback - the same label is written 'SN2'.
findings.learner_impact: Minor, but it is the one mechanism label the chapter borrows from earlier chapters, and an inconsistent or mangled rendering in the reader undermines the deliberate cross-chapter link the sentence is making.
findings.evidence: package occurrences: 'S_N2' x1 (nugget prose), 'SN2' x2 (ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability option and feedback); compiled reader contains 'S_N2' twice.
findings.recommended_outcome: One SN2 rendering should be used throughout prose, options and feedback, and it must be one that survives the markdown pipeline into the reader.

location.anchor_text: Name the functional group that this step converts into an ester, thereby retiring the chains that carry it.

findings.observation: The accepted-answer list for ch28-capping-purpose contains only variants that include the 5' locant ('the unreacted 5'-hydroxyl', '5'-OH', '5' hydroxyl', and so on). A student who answers the question exactly as asked - 'the hydroxyl group', 'a free hydroxyl', 'an alcohol' - is marked wrong even though the prompt asks for the functional group rather than its position, and even though only one kind of free hydroxyl exists on the support at that point in the cycle.
findings.learner_impact: A short-answer item that autogrades a correct answer as wrong erodes trust in the bank and, on this concept, punishes the student who has understood capping but not guessed the required phrasing.
findings.evidence: ch28-capping-purpose answer_key [redacted].
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the accepted-answer set must cover the answer the prompt literally asks for, or the prompt must ask for the position as well as the group.

strengths: Every SMILES in the package is chemically correct on independent RDKit verification: 20/20 parse, and the InChIKeys of adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine, uracil, beta-D-ribofuranose, 2-deoxy-beta-D-ribofuranose, adenosine, 2'-deoxyadenosine, thymidine, cytidine, uridine, dAMP, ATP, zidovudine, acyclovir and 2',3'-dideoxyadenosine all match the authentic compounds, including the stereochemistry.

The beta-N-glycosidic configuration is right in every nucleoside, and the CIP descriptors that change between related structures (C3' S->R on cyclisation to the 2',3'-cyclic phosphate, C4' R->S in dideoxyadenosine and zidovudine) are all priority-swap artefacts rather than configurational errors - the underlying D-sugar geometry is preserved throughout.

The dinucleotide mol-dinucleotide-dapdt is genuinely dA(3'->5')dT: free 5'-OH on the deoxyadenosine residue, phosphate bridging its 3'-oxygen to the thymidine 5'-oxygen, free 3'-OH on the thymidine. Directionality and the 'never the 2' position' rule are both structurally enforced, not merely asserted.

The RNA cleavage account is mechanistically complete and correct: deprotonation to the 2'-alkoxide, in-line attack on the phosphorus of its own 3'-phosphodiester, departure of the neighbouring 5'-oxygen, a cis-fused five-membered 2',3'-cyclic phosphate (which embeds cleanly in 3D), and opening at either ester bond to the 2'/3' monophosphate mixture that is correctly identified as the classical evidence for the intermediate.

Chain extension is correctly placed at the alpha phosphorus with pyrophosphate as leaving group, in-line through a trigonal bipyramid with inversion, two-metal-ion assistance correctly divided, and - unusually well handled - the substitution itself identified as close to thermoneutral with pyrophosphate hydrolysis named as the actual driving force. Both hotspot answer keys point at the correct atom.

The lactam/lactim treatment is exactly right and, crucially, refuses the usual bad argument: the chapter states plainly that both tautomers are aromatic so aromaticity cannot decide it, and settles the question on amide-versus-enol bonding. The donor/acceptor consequences are then read off correctly for both legitimate pairs and both rejected ones.

The chapter repeatedly corrects standard oversimplifications rather than propagating them - hydrogen bonding supplies specificity while stacking supplies stability; GC melting is not just a hydrogen-bond count; melting temperature is meaningless without stating the buffer; direction of growth is a consequence of where the activation sits, demonstrated by contrasting the polymerase with the 3'-to-5' phosphoramidite cycle.

Wrong-answer explanations teach rather than scold, and several are genuinely excellent - the cAMP distractor explanation, the 3'-amino chain-terminator explanation (small enough but still nucleophilic, giving a phosphoramidate), and the capping explanation that capping does not improve yield but converts a hard purification into an easy one.
Twelve question types across ten concepts with 23 distinct stems, each with a differentiated v2, three-level hint ladders on every item, and structure-bearing options on the identification questions.
open_questions: The 1BNA figure is served from an external CDN (https://cdn.rcsb.org/images/structures/1bna_assembly-1.jpeg) rather than from the repo. Since the reader is an installable PWA, is that image expected to be available offline, and is the chapter's only atomic-resolution duplex figure acceptable as a remote dependency?

practice_check prompts and answers exist on all ten nuggets and are strong (the pH-3 depurination one and the 5'-ATG-3' directionality one especially), but they do not appear as blocks in the compiled reader. Which surface shows them to students, and does an instructor assigning the reader alone get them at all?

All four video briefs are production_status 'deferred' and compile to hidden blocks with empty URLs. Is the deferral expected to persist through publication, in which case the base-pairing and mechanism content needs a non-video carrier (see instr-002, instr-003), or is production scheduled?

ch28-rna-stability-error-repair and its v2 rely on the grader consuming target_id / category_id / repair_option_id; earlier chapters in this corpus recorded that error_repair keys do not reach the grader. Has that been resolved, and are these two items actually autogradable as authored?

ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot keys 'atom_15' and its v2 keys 'atom_7'; both are correct against RDKit's 0-based atom indices for the given SMILES. Is that indexing contract guaranteed by the renderer, or could canonicalisation at render time shift it?

personas.summary: The prose in this chapter is unusually good for a shaky student: it repeatedly refuses to let me memorise, names the wrong move before I make it ("Hydrogen bonding is not what holds the duplex together", "Students look for the reactive carbon and there is not one"), and every one of the 23 surfaced questions carries a genuinely progressive three-level hint ladder plus wrong-answer explanations that diagnose the specific error rather than restating the prompt. Where I stall is the visual layer, and I stall in exactly the places the chapter itself says are the important ones. The base-pairing section is built entirely on "bring the two edges together" and "reading down adenine's pairing edge", but the page shows four unrelated base structures in independent orientations and nothing that shows two bases facing each other; the asset meant to fix that is a video whose url is empty. The two mechanisms in the chapter — the 2'-alkoxide cutting RNA, and the 3'-hydroxyl attacking the alpha phosphorus — have no mechanism drawing at all, even though the text tells me the RNA one "is worth drawing for yourself rather than reading". Every figure caption asks me to find C2', C3', N9 or the 3'-oxygen, and not one figure carries those numbers. The phosphoramidite section is the densest text in the chapter and its only figure is an image block with url:"" — it renders as nothing. There is no self-check anywhere inside the reader (the well-written practice_check for each nugget never reaches the compiled chapter), no objectives or depth labels to tell me which of the ten sections are core and which are advanced, and four of the ten concepts have no core-difficulty question to start me off — nucleoside-analogue-drugs has exactly one question in the whole bank and it is an advanced two-field structured_reasoning. I would finish this chapter feeling like I had read something very clear and still be unable to draw a base pair.

location.anchor_text: Bring the two edges together and the pattern reads donor-acceptor against acceptor-donor.

findings.observation: The entire section is written as an instruction to perform a spatial operation on two structures at once — "Reading down adenine's pairing edge", "Bring the two edges together", "Acceptor-donor-donor faces donor-acceptor-acceptor" — but nothing on the page shows two bases facing one another. The reader section contains four independent molecule blocks (mol-adenine, mol-thymine, mol-guanine, mol-cytosine), each rendered from SMILES in whatever orientation the layout engine chooses, so their 'pairing edges' do not point at anything. The only asset that was meant to show a pair, video-base-pairing ("Reading donors and acceptors into a base pair"), has production_status "deferred" and compiles into the reader with url: "".
findings.learner_impact: I cannot do the operation the text is describing, so I fall back on the exact behaviour the concept's own trouble_spots warn against — memorising "A goes with T, G goes with C, two bonds and three bonds" — and then guess on ch28-pairing-donors-acceptors and ch28-mismatch-failure-mode, which are graded on reading the pattern off structures rather than recalling it. The A-with-C failure ("puts adenine's exocyclic NH2 opposite cytosine's exocyclic NH2") is even harder: I am asked to visualise a pair that is never drawn even in words' worth of geometry.

location.anchor_text: neighbouring-group participation**, and it is worth drawing for yourself rather than reading.

findings.observation: Both mechanisms in the chapter are taught with no mechanism representation of any kind. The RNA cleavage section states the mechanism "is worth drawing for yourself rather than reading" and its learning objective is "Draw the mechanism by which base cleaves an RNA backbone through the 2'-alkoxide and a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate intermediate", yet the section's assets are static endpoint structures only (mol-uridine, mol-uridine-23-cyclic-phosphate, mol-dinucleotide-dapdt) plus a deferred video with url: "". The compiled chapter contains no reaction, reaction_coordinate or curved-arrow block of any type (block-type census: text 10, molecule 34, image 4, video 4, external_link 10, mcmurry_link 1).

I skip the drawing, re-read the paragraph instead, and arrive at ch28-rna-cleavage-intermediate having to choose between a five-membered 2',3'-cyclic phosphate and a six-membered 3',5'-cyclic phosphate purely from a verbal atom count ("O2', C2', C3', O3' and P") in hint level 2 — which is where I guess.

The stated objectives ask for drawing, so the chapter has to model the drawing at least once.

location.anchor_text: Count the three hydroxyls at C2', C3', and C5' and note the anomeric carbon that will bond to a base.

findings.observation: Every molecule block in the chapter carries a reading instruction phrased in primed locants, but the rendered figure is a bare SMILES depiction with no atom numbering. Examples: "Count the three hydroxyls at C2', C3', and C5'" (mol-beta-d-ribofuranose), "Trace the bond from N9 of adenine to C1' of ribose" (mol-adenosine), "Trace one phosphate esterified twice - to the 3' oxygen of one residue and the 5' oxygen of the next" (mol-dinucleotide-dapdt), "Identify the alpha phosphorus... and the beta and gamma pair" (mol-atp). Learning the primed numbering system is itself one of the chapter's first objectives ("State what the prime marks in a locant such as C3'"), so the reader cannot be assumed to already know which ring carbon is which.
findings.learner_impact: I look at the picture, cannot tell which carbon is C2' versus C3', and either invent an assignment or stop trying to use the figures at all and read only the prose. That damage compounds: the 2'-versus-3' distinction is the whole content of the RNA-stability section, the 3'-versus-5' distinction is the whole content of the backbone and chain-extension sections, and the alpha/beta/gamma labels are what ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot is graded on.
findings.evidence: Reader block content for mol-beta-d-ribofuranose, mol-2-deoxy-beta-d-ribofuranose, mol-adenosine, mol-damp, mol-dinucleotide-dapdt, mol-atp — each has keys alt_text, description, generator_href, name, smiles and no labelling data. Nugget objective: "State what the prime marks in a locant such as C3', and use primed and unprimed numbers without confusing sugar positions with base positions."
findings.recommended_outcome: At least the first sugar, the first nucleoside, the dinucleotide and the triphosphate need their positions identified on the figure itself, so that the numbering convention the chapter is teaching can be read off a picture rather than assumed. Without that, every instruction of the form 'find C3'' is unfollowable.

location.anchor_text: One turn of the phosphoramidite synthesis cycle

location.anchor_text: Count the three hydroxyls at C2', C3', and C5'

findings.observation: Every nugget carries a well-written practice_check with a model answer — ten of them, and they are the best scaffolding in the package (e.g. the cytidine 5'-monophosphate disassembly, the pH 3 depurination account, the 5'-ATG-3' directionality walk-through). A low-confidence student in that situation reads the whole chapter, feels that it made sense, and then cannot start question one.

location.anchor_text: Dilute NaOH cuts RNA in minutes

findings.observation: The reader carries no per-section learning objectives, no depth label and no time estimate, so all ten sections read as equally required. The package has all three on every nugget (three learning_objectives each; depth core / standard / advanced; duration_minutes 6–8), but the compiled section object has only the keys id, title and blocks. Nothing tells a reader that nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy is core and reading-and-writing-dna is advanced. The chapter also carries a single McMurry/OpenStax link, in section 1 only, and it points at the generic "28-why-this-chapter" landing page rather than at any specific section.

When I do want a second explanation of, say, base pairing, there is no section-level textbook link to go to.

findings.observation: The difficulty ladder has no bottom rung on most of the chapter. Of ten concepts, only three have a core-difficulty question (nucleoside-and-nucleotide-anatomy, purine-and-pyrimidine-bases, n-glycosidic-bond). nucleoside-analogue-drugs has exactly one question in the entire bank and it is ch28-chain-terminator-design, an advanced structured_reasoning item with two required fields and nine options. reading-and-writing-dna has two questions, both advanced. phosphodiester-backbone opens on a numeric charge count; base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding has three questions, all standard, the first a six-option multi_select.
findings.learner_impact: On four of the ten concepts my first contact with assessment is an item that assumes I already have the whole picture. I have no cheap win to confirm I understood the basics of, for example, what a chain terminator is, before being asked to design one and defend the design — so I guess on the claim field, get the evidence field wrong too, and read the result as 'I do not understand this topic' rather than 'I skipped a rung'.

location.anchor_text: raising the salt concentration of a solution raises the melting temperature of a duplex by screening that repulsion

findings.observation: "Melting temperature" is used as a load-bearing quantity from section 4 onwards and is never defined anywhere in the chapter prose. It first appears in the phosphodiester-backbone section — three sections before the duplex has been described at all — then in the base-pairing section ("a GC-rich sequence melts at a higher temperature") and repeatedly in the double-helix section. The only place the chapter says what melting actually is appears inside a wrong-answer explanation on an advanced question: "Melting a duplex separates the strands without breaking a single covalent bond" (ch28-duplex-stability-reasoning, claim_covalent). "Anneal" is likewise used without introduction.
findings.learner_impact: I meet 'melting temperature' before I have met the double helix, so I have no referent for what is melting; the everyday sense of the word points me at a phase change or at bonds breaking. That wrong model survives into ch28-melting-temperature-rank, where I am asked to order four duplexes by Tm and I am ranking a quantity I cannot picture, and into the salt-screening argument, which only makes sense once you know the two strands come apart.
findings.evidence: Occurrences of "melt" in the compiled reader text: sections nugget-phosphodiester-backbone, nugget-base-pairing-and-hydrogen-bonding, nugget-dna-double-helix-and-base-stacking (x3); no definition present. Definition appears only in feedback_bundle.wrong_answer_explanations of ch28-duplex-stability-reasoning.
findings.recommended_outcome: A student needs 'melting' named as strand separation at the point of first use, and ideally not before the duplex exists in the chapter, so that the melting-temperature arguments and the ranking question rest on a picture rather than a word.

location.anchor_text: In a Haworth-style drawing with the furanose ring in the plane of the paper, the ring oxygen at the back, and the C5' group pointing up, beta means the base also points up

findings.observation: Beta configuration is defined exclusively in terms of a drawing convention the chapter never shows. The text specifies a Haworth-style depiction with a stated ring orientation, and the mol-adenosine block description then tells the student to "confirm the base sits on the same face of the ring as the 5' group" — but the figure is an RDKit render from the SMILES Nc1ncnc2c1ncn2[C@@H]1O[C@H](CO)[C@@H](O)[C@H]1O, which is not a Haworth projection and whose ring orientation is not controlled. The chapter contains no Haworth-style figure at all.
findings.learner_impact: I am given a test ('same face as C5'') and a picture the test does not apply to, so I either read the wedge/dash pattern wrong or decide beta is a naming rule I have to memorise — which is exactly the trouble spot the concept lists ('treating the anomeric configuration as a free choice rather than a fixed structural fact'). The chapter then tells me this is a real stereochemical statement, and I have no way to verify it for myself.
findings.evidence: Reader section nugget-n-glycosidic-bond text block; block description for mol-adenosine: "Trace the bond from N9 of adenine to C1' of ribose and confirm the base sits on the same face of the ring as the 5' group."; asset mol-adenosine has only a smiles field, no depiction style. Objective: "Assign the beta configuration at the anomeric carbon and explain what beta means in terms of the face the base occupies relative to C5'."
findings.recommended_outcome: A student needs the alpha/beta distinction shown in the same representation the definition uses, with both anomers side by side, so that 'same face as C5'' is something that can be checked on the page rather than accepted on trust.

location.anchor_text: Treat with acetic anhydride and N-methylimidazole

findings.observation: The rank_order question names each step by a reagent recipe rather than by the name the prose uses, and two of those recipes are not in the chapter. "N-methylimidazole" appears nowhere in the topic package or the reader at all. "Dichloroacetic acid in dichloromethane" appears exactly once, in the expanded tier only — a reader who has lowered the detail level (a natural move when a section feels dense) sees only "Mild acid removes it". When the order is wrong I get a paragraph telling me to work out what each reagent does — the same thing I just failed at — rather than being told which two cards I swapped.

location.anchor_text: the reverse reaction has a name, pyrophosphorolysis

The aniline comparison that the correct option of ch28-base-weak-basicity depends on ("conjugated into the ring from an exocyclic NH2 as in aniline") likewise appears only in expanded. The pyrrole-type / pyridine-type distinction that ch28-pairing-donors-acceptors option f is scored on is defined only in expanded; the standard tier drops the phrase "pyridine-type ring nitrogens" with no explanation of what makes a ring nitrogen pyridine-type.

I take the shorter version because I am struggling, then fail the questions because I was struggling — and nothing warns me that the shorter tier is not assessment-complete.

location.anchor_text: The structure shown is an incoming nucleoside 5'-triphosphate

findings.observation: The hotspot question renders adenosine 5'-triphosphate — a ribose with hydroxyls at both C2' and C3' — as "the incoming nucleoside 5'-triphosphate" at a DNA-flavoured growing end, immediately after two sections whose central claim is that the DNA sugar has no 2'-hydroxyl and that this is why DNA survives. Nothing in the prompt or the surrounding prose flags that this particular structure is the RNA/transcription case.
findings.learner_impact: Having just been told that the presence or absence of one hydroxyl is the difference between a genome and a disposable message, I see a structure with that hydroxyl presented as the monomer for chain growth and either conclude I had the DNA/RNA distinction backwards, or decide the distinction does not matter much after all. Either way the one fact the chapter worked hardest to install gets loosened.

location.anchor_text: Everything established about glycoside reactivity transfers, and it is worth transferring deliberately rather than learning the nucleoside case as a separate fact.

findings.observation: The chapter's key reactivity arguments are handed off to earlier chapters by assertion rather than by bridge. The acid/base behaviour of the glycosidic bond rests entirely on "That makes it an N,O-acetal" plus "Everything established about glycoside reactivity transfers" — acetals are never re-characterised in the chapter, and the anomeric carbon's stability to base is asserted rather than derived on the page. Similarly, the tautomer argument that decides every base pair rests on "for the same reason an ordinary amide does not sit as its enol" with no restatement of that reason, the backbone section leans on "the closest relative is a polyester", and the basicity argument leans on aromatic-amine conjugation. All four are prerequisite chapters (carbohydrates, carbonyl chemistry, esters, aromaticity/amines) invoked by name without a refresher.
findings.learner_impact: If any one of those earlier chapters did not stick — and for me they did not all stick — the sentence lands as a fact to memorise rather than as a transfer, which is exactly what the text says it does not want. On ch28-glycoside-acid-base-stability I then have to decide whether hydroxide can attack C1' with no working model of why acetals are base-stable, so I pick the option that sounds most like a mechanism I recognise.
findings.evidence: Reader section nugget-n-glycosidic-bond: "That makes it an **N,O-acetal**... Everything established about glycoside reactivity transfers"; nugget-purine-and-pyrimidine-bases: "for the same reason an ordinary amide does not sit as its enol"; nugget-phosphodiester-backbone: "the closest relative is a polyester". Concepts[] prerequisites list only within-chapter slugs — no cross-chapter prerequisites are recorded anywhere in the package.
findings.recommended_outcome: A student needs a one- or two-sentence in-place refresher at each of these hand-off points — what an acetal is and why base cannot touch it, and why the amide form beats the enol — so that 'transfer it deliberately' is an instruction I can actually carry out rather than a reminder of what I have forgotten.

strengths: Every one of the 23 surfaced questions carries a complete three-level hint ladder, and the hints genuinely teach a route forward instead of restating the prompt — ch28-backbone-charge-count moves from 'charge comes only from phosphorus' to 'twelve beads need eleven links' to the pKa argument, and ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot's level-2 hint highlights C4', C5' and the 5'-oxygen on the structure itself.

Wrong-answer explanations diagnose the specific wrong move rather than saying 'not quite': ch28-purine-pyrimidine-sort names the error as 'sorting on substituents', ch28-mismatch-failure-mode explains that size is precisely what is not wrong with A·C, and ch28-melting-temperature-rank tells a student whose ladder is inverted that every comparison was right and only the direction was wrong.

The prose names the misconception before the student makes it, in bold and in advance: 'Hydrogen bonding is not what holds the duplex together', 'Students look for the reactive carbon and there is not one', 'capping does not increase the yield of correct full-length product at all'. That is exactly the move a shaky reader needs.

The chapter consistently frames rules as derivable rather than memorisable and then actually does the derivation in the text (the two-condition argument for base pairing, the n-minus-one charge count, the alpha-versus-beta-versus-gamma argument), so there is a model of the reasoning even where the figure is missing.

Each molecule block carries a 'description' telling the reader what to look for in that structure rather than just naming it — a genuine reading instruction, and the reason the missing atom labels in stu-003 are frustrating rather than fatal.
open_questions: The brief for this review stated that the reader shows the standard tier by default, but [internal source reference — not in this repo] sets detailLevel: "expanded" as the default and the compiled block markdown is the expanded text. I have written stu-011 on the assumption that expanded is the default and that lowering the tier is the risk; if the default is in fact standard, stu-011 becomes considerably more severe.

Empty video urls appear to be the platform norm at this stage (biomolecules-carbohydrates, biomolecules-lipids and amines-and-heterocycles all have zero non-empty video urls), so stu-001 and stu-002 are written about the missing mechanism/base-pair representation rather than about the video pipeline itself. The empty image url in stu-004, by contrast, is specific to this chapter — its other three image blocks resolve.

practice_check never reaching the compiled reader (stu-005) and sections carrying no objectives or depth (stu-006) both look like schema-level limitations rather than authoring omissions — the compiled section object only supports id/title/blocks. Is a reader-side checkpoint or objective surface planned, or should the practice_check content be re-expressed as reader blocks?

The reader-side .questions.json exposes only prompt_text and metadata (no student_config, answer_key or feedback_bundle), matching live chapters such as ethers-epoxides-thiols-and-sulfides. I have assumed the hints and wrong-answer explanations I reviewed do reach the student through the seeded bank rather than this file; if they do not, most of what I listed as strengths is invisible to the learner.

Should ch28-base-pair-comparison show both partners? It renders only the purine of each pair and names the pyrimidine in text, which asks a struggling student to recall thymine and cytosine from memory in a question about reading structures — I judged this too minor to file, but it points the same way as stu-001.

personas.summary: The authored accessibility metadata in this package is among the best I have reviewed: every one of the 24 assets carries both an alt_text and a long_description that convey real chemistry (ring sizes, numbered positions, stereocentre counts, donor/acceptor patterns) and that are honest about what the image does NOT show, and all 46 questions carry an accessible_description that describes the stimulus and the task without leaking the answer. Nothing in the prose or the items depends on colour, motion, hover, or spatial position as a sole carrier of meaning; the two colour mentions are chemistry facts, not required distinctions. The deferred video briefs are handled well — their production notes pre-commit to captions, transcripts, and narration that names every visual change, and the compiled reader marks all four video blocks is_hidden so no learner meets an unproduced media stub. The problems are all in delivery, not authoring. Two required activity types cannot be completed without sight and a pointing device: the two hotspot items expose atom targets whose only accessible names are element-plus-index ("P atom 16"), with no mapping from any chemical position named in the prompt or the description to a specific target, and the two structure_scaffold items offer no answer channel except an embedded Ketcher drawing canvas. Compounding both, the authored accessible_description is not surfaced by the renderers that serve these question types, and the compiler drops every asset long_description on the way into the reader, so the richest non-visual descriptions in the package never reach a learner. A smaller structural defect: the reader's RichText renderer does not implement markdown headings or ordered lists, so the longest section emits literal "###" strings and loses its only heading landmarks.

location.anchor_text: Select the phosphorus atom that the free 3'-hydroxyl of the growing strand attacks.

findings.observation: Both hotspot items (ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot, ch28-alpha-phosphorus-hotspot-v2) require selecting one specific heavy atom on a rendered structure. The atom targets are real keyboard-focusable buttons — that part is fine — but their only accessible name is generated as `${atom.symbol} atom ${atom.index + 1}` from the RDKit heavy-atom index ([internal source reference — not in this repo]). For the ATP stimulus the three phosphorus targets announce as "P atom 16", "P atom 20", "P atom 24"; the answer key is atom_15, the alpha phosphorus. Nothing in the prompt, the student_config, the rendered payload (atoms carry only id/index/x/y/symbol — [internal source reference — not in this repo]), or the accessible_description maps a chemical position (alpha phosphorus, C5', the free 3'-hydroxyl) onto an atom number. A learner who cannot see the drawing knows exactly which atom is chemically correct and still cannot tell which button it is; the only way to recover the mapping is to know the SMILES traversal order, which is never disclosed. location.anchor_text: ### Reading: Sanger sequencing

findings.observation: The reader's RichText component implements only paragraph splitting, **bold**, and `code` — it has no handling for markdown headings or lists. The default (expanded) text of nugget-reading-and-writing-dna contains three `###` subheadings and a four-item numbered list, so the longest section of the chapter renders "### Reading: Sanger sequencing", "### Writing: the phosphoramidite cycle", and "### Why the direction is reversed" as literal paragraph text, and "1. **Detritylation.** … 2. **Coupling.** … 3. **Capping.** … 4. **Oxidation.**" as four ordinary paragraphs. The document heading outline is therefore h1 (chapter) → h2 (section) → h4 (structure card names) with nothing in between, and the section's internal structure is invisible to assistive technology.
findings.learner_impact: Screen reader users navigating by heading cannot jump to the sequencing or synthesis subsections of the chapter's densest section and must read it linearly. The list semantics that would announce "list of 4 items, item 1 of 4" are lost, which matters here because the four steps are an ordered cycle and the chapter's rank_order item assesses exactly that order. Sighted learners also see raw "###" characters, and the h2→h4 jump is a heading-order irregularity for everyone.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] (regex handles only `**` and backticks; paragraphs split on blank lines). Compiled reader nugget-reading-and-writing-dna markdown contains three `### …` lines and `1.`–`4.` list markers. StructureCard uses `Heading as="h4"`; TopicPackageChapterRenderer uses h1 for the chapter and h2 for each section.
findings.recommended_outcome: The subsection and step structure the author wrote needs to survive into the rendered page as real structure a learner can navigate and an assistive technology can announce, in correct heading order.

location.anchor_text: Click an atom to circle it; click a bonded neighbor to grow the circle

findings.observation: Three smaller issues in the same workspace. (b) The workspace instruction is pointer-only phrasing ("Click an atom to circle it; click a bonded neighbor to grow the circle; click a distant atom to start over"), which is both inaccurate for keyboard users and the only place the growth behaviour is explained. (c) The selection readout that names the current selection ("selected: P16") sits in a plain <Text>, not an aria-live region, so a screen reader user who activates a target hears the button's own aria-pressed change but gets no announcement of the resulting selection set.
findings.learner_impact: A keyboard or screen reader user exploring the targets by activating them — the natural way to find out what is there when you cannot see the drawing — silently builds a multi-atom answer on an item that expects one atom, and gets no announced confirmation of what is currently selected. Combined with access-001 this makes the workspace not just hard to answer but hard to inspect safely.

strengths: Every one of the 24 assets carries both alt_text and long_description, and they describe chemistry rather than naming the picture — ring sizes, numbered ring positions, which nitrogen bonds to the sugar, stereocentre counts, and the donor/acceptor pattern along each pairing edge.

The image descriptions are explicitly honest about their own limits: clip-dna-double-helix states it 'does not depict individual atoms, the two grooves of differing width, or which base occupies any particular rung', and pdb-b-dna-dodecamer states it 'is a still rendering and conveys no motion or colour-coded sequence information'.

All 46 questions carry an accessible_description; none leaks the answer, and each names the task precisely. Text-only items say so explicitly ('no structures are shown'), which spares a screen reader user hunting for a figure that does not exist.

No distinction anywhere in the chapter rests on colour, motion, hover, or spatial position alone. The only colour references are chemistry facts (the orange DMT cation as a coupling-efficiency readout, the four-dye Sanger trace) and both are explained in words.

The base-pairing section deliberately carries no visual-only pairing diagram: donor/acceptor patterns are stated in prose and repeated in each base's alt text, so nothing about A·T versus G·C is available only to a viewer.

The deferred video briefs record their accessibility requirements up front — closed captions, narration naming every visual change, a text transcript, and an explicit rule that 'no distinction in this brief may rest on colour, highlight, or motion alone' — and each notes which reader nugget carries the same content.

rank_order, categorize_groups, matching_pairs, comparison_matrix and error_repair are all keyboard-complete by construction: native <Select> per item, native radios, a semantic table with scope'd headers, and move-up/move-down buttons with an aria-live position readout rather than drag-only reordering.

The hotspot's level-2 hints name the highlighted atoms in words ('Highlighted are the sugar's C4' and C5' carbons together with the 5'-oxygen'), so the hint ladder does not depend on seeing the highlight.

personas.summary: This chapter is figure-dense by count and figure-poor where it matters. Thirty-three molecule blocks (from 20 unique assets), two clipart drawings, one crystal-structure still and one roadmap are distributed across ten sections, and the individual structures are well chosen and carefully alt-texted. But almost every idea in the chapter that is inherently spatial is carried by prose alone: no figure anywhere shows two bases hydrogen bonded to each other, none shows antiparallel strand direction or the 120-degree glycosidic-bond geometry that produces the two grooves, and none shows the in-line attack geometry at phosphorus that both mechanisms in the chapter turn on. Two media containers ship broken — four video blocks compile with an empty url and a stage-direction sentence as their description, and the phosphoramidite roadmap compiles to an image block with url "" so its fully authored five-node, four-step spec never reaches a student. Compounding this, the reader renders plain skeletal structures with no atom numbering while nearly every caption instructs the reader to "locate N9", "identify the 2' hydroxyl", or "identify the alpha phosphorus" — the picture cannot answer the question its own caption asks. Layout works against the figures too: each section is one 3000-7000 character text block followed by a stack of unlabelled structures, so no figure is ever adjacent to the sentence it supports. The deliberate omission of a reaction-coordinate diagram is correct and should be kept; the omission of any arrow-pushing or geometry figure is not. Direction of fix is as much subtraction as addition — several structures repeat verbatim three and four times in sections where they teach nothing new.

location.anchor_text: Identify the alpha phosphorus that a growing chain attacks, and the beta and gamma pair that leave together as pyrophosphate.

findings.observation: Nearly every molecule caption instructs the reader to find a numbered position, but the reader renders plain skeletal structures with no atom numbering, no position labels, and no highlighting. The reader's molecule block content carries only name, smiles, alt_text, description and generator_href; the shared render preferences file states explicitly that "Wedge/dash bonds and atom indices are never exposed to viewers", and none of the 20 molecule assets in this package authors any per-figure rdkit_options or highlight.

A reader told to "identify the alpha phosphorus" sees three chemically identical-looking P atoms in a row with nothing distinguishing them; told to "locate N9" sees five unlabelled nitrogens; told to "identify the 2' hydroxyl" sees three unlabelled hydroxyls on a furanose. The reader who could already do this without the figure does not need it, and the reader who needs it cannot use it — which inverts the point of having a figure at all.
